title: 1.1 · One object, different readings
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · SESSION 1.1 · CYCLE 1

One object, different readings

110-minute long session · B+C double block

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

tr.u1.repeat. I can describe the spread in measurements and propose a check that explains a disagreement.

Drawing / representation evidence: tr.u1.sketch — Sketch your object. Label its measured length, unit and endpoints. If you drew on paper, use this canvas for a simple matching outline with the length. Mark the drawing NTS (not to scale).

Success today: Opening: choice 2. Range check: choice 1. Practice highest 15 11/16, lowest 15 9/16, spread 1/8 in. A fair test changes one factor: for example the observer reads the same tool at the same endpoints directly above and then at an angle. Do not promise a particular result. A systematic offset may remain even with zero spread.

THE FIELDHOUSE THREAD TODAY

What students know as today opens: Students begin without a shared measurement method.

How today connects: A replacement part needs a dimension another person can trust; establish the evidence routine for the fieldhouse survey.

Lesson Flow

Use the 110-minute sequence below. Timings include discussion, transitions and collection.

TimeWhat happens

0–10 min

Diagnostic opening

Teacher: Open the lesson in Present and show its first diagram. Ask: “Two people report different lengths for the same object. What can you conclude now?” Collect an individual choice and reason before discussion. Reveal: The measurements disagree; we need to check the method and tools..

Students produce: A saved opening response; then 60 seconds of partner explanation using the diagram.

Look/listen for: Agreement proves accuracy. Ask students to compare a repeated reading against a separate checked reference. Keep the spread and the reference offset as different quantities.

10–25 min

Explain and model

Teacher: Model aloud: Highest: 15 11/16 in. Lowest: 15 9/16 in. 15 11/16 − 15 9/16 = 2/16 in Spread = 1/8 in. This is observed variation, not a certified uncertainty. Ask a student to identify the reference, the unit and the evidence supporting the conclusion.

Students produce: An annotated calculation or reference sketch with quantities and units; a prediction before the investigation.

Look/listen for: A reason for each operation. If students repeat the answer without a method, cover the result and have them point to the given quantities.

25–45 min

Investigation and individual record

Teacher: Set up: Ruler or tape per student or pair; rigid object; removable tape; paper and pencils. No fieldhouse access or caliper required. Direct the sequence: 1. Choose a tabletop edge, rigid book cover, wood offcut or accessible block. Name the object and mark the two endpoints with removable tape. 2. Check where zero is on the tool. A ruler’s physical edge may not be zero. 3. Keep the tool straight and look directly above the endpoint. Read the smallest marked division you can use reliably. 4. Lift and replace the tool for each of three readings. Record the fraction and unit. Repeated identical readings are possible. Rotate measurement/checking roles; observe each student rather than inferring skill from a group result.

Students produce: An individual table with quantities, values, units and evidence source. Label supplied data as supplied; keep unexpected results.

Look/listen for: Ask students to compare a repeated reading against a separate checked reference. Keep the spread and the reference offset as different quantities.

45–50 min

Stop and check the evidence

Teacher: Pause work, reset tools and compare one example from two students. Ask what was held fixed and whether the recorded values support the claim. Re-model the specific error if needed.

Students produce: A marked correction or a named check to perform next; a brief transition before the second investigation.

Look/listen for: The original result remains visible; a correction includes a reason.

50–70 min

Test an explanation

Teacher: Use this follow-up: Ask students to compare a repeated reading against a separate checked reference. Keep the spread and the reference offset as different quantities. Students name one plausible explanation, predict a result and change one relevant factor or compare an independent method. With paper data, test an alternate interpretation of the same stated constraints; do not invent observations.

Students produce: A second evidence record and an explanation of what the comparison supports or leaves unresolved.

Look/listen for: Agreement proves accuracy must be addressed with evidence, not replaced by a new unsupported claim.

70–90 min

Drawing and handoff

Teacher: Assign: Sketch your object. Label its measured length, unit and endpoints. If you drew on paper, use this canvas for a simple matching outline with the length. Mark the drawing NTS (not to scale). Partners exchange without an oral explanation first. The reader identifies the datum/endpoints, units and one missing or ambiguous label; the author revises.

Students produce: An individual labelled drawing or setup record, with NTS or a verified scale and a visible revision.

Look/listen for: The representation agrees with the measurements and can be interpreted without the author supplying missing information.

90–103 min

Individual exit and evidence

Teacher: Ask the exact lesson exit: “Use your readings (or label the provided practice data). State the highest and lowest, calculate the spread with units, name one possible cause of disagreement, and describe one fair check. What result would support your explanation?” Allow the existing frame and word bank; require the same reasoning from every student. Collect before discussing the key.

Students produce: An individual saved exit response or named paper response. Keep observations of actual tool use distinct from supplied-data reasoning.

Look/listen for: Expected response: Opening: choice 2. Range check: choice 1. Practice highest 15 11/16, lowest 15 9/16, spread 1/8 in. A fair test changes one factor: for example the observer reads the same tool at the same endpoints directly above and then at an angle. Do not promise a particular result. A systematic offset may remain even with zero spread.

103–110 min

Feedback, revision and next lesson

Teacher: Return one specific next step. Use the target criteria below; do not turn self-ratings or a correct opening choice into a mastery grade. If the lesson has a self-assessment, complete it after the individual exit. Collect tools and preserve original evidence.

Students produce: A next-check statement and any self-assessment already present in the lesson; teacher notes identify who needs a short recheck.

Look/listen for: A missing response remains not observed, not an invented low score. Begin the next meeting by checking the misconception named below.

IF THE SCHEDULE IS SHORTENED

Protect the individual exit. In a 55-minute version: 0–7 opening; 7–17 model; 17–30 one investigation; 30–40 drawing; 40–50 exit; 50–55 feedback. Schedule the independent follow-up check next time; do not mark practical performance complete from the abbreviated or supplied-data route.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Opening answer: The measurements disagree; we need to check the method and tools.

Specific misconception: Agreement proves accuracy

Teacher response: Ask students to compare a repeated reading against a separate checked reference. Keep the spread and the reference offset as different quantities.

Exit prompt: Use your readings (or label the provided practice data). State the highest and lowest, calculate the spread with units, name one possible cause of disagreement, and describe one fair check. What result would support your explanation?

Expected evidence / answer: Opening: choice 2. Range check: choice 1. Practice highest 15 11/16, lowest 15 9/16, spread 1/8 in. A fair test changes one factor: for example the observer reads the same tool at the same endpoints directly above and then at an angle. Do not promise a particular result. A systematic offset may remain even with zero spread.

Additional checkpoint: For those practice data, which conclusion is supported?

Answer: The spread is 1/8 inch.

Teacher 1–2–3 criteria: Rate tr.u1.repeat: 1 = cannot yet identify endpoints/high-low or proposes an unrelated check; 2 = gives a usable spread or plausible cause but needs help with units/control/evidence; 3 = accurate spread with units plus a plausible cause and a controlled check with a predicted discriminating result. Rate sketch separately only from the individual artifact. Use no evidence/not observed rather than inventing a low skill score for absent students.

Rate only the named target from the actual individual evidence. Assess the physics rather than grammar, spelling or use of a scaffold. No evidence / not observed is distinct from an incorrect demonstration. Student self-ratings remain separate.

MATERIALS & READING

Prepare before class: Ruler or tape per student or pair; rigid object; removable tape; paper and pencils. No fieldhouse access or caliper required.

In the application: 1.1 · One object, different readings (tu1-s01). Open the same lesson in Present; use its diagram, supplied data, procedure and response prompts.

Print / reference: Opening-Cycle Student Packet, the session 1.1 activity; Session 1.1 uses pages 1–2. The lesson itself contains the prompts and supplied values if the local packet is unavailable.

Drawing Book assignment: Use the lesson diagram and any assigned drawing prompt; no additional textbook reading required.

If materials or access are unavailable: No tool: use the clearly labelled practice readings for reasoning and the drawing task. Do not record instrument-use mastery from supplied data. No internet: paper packet contains the same prompts and scoring criteria.

TEACHER NOTES

Before students arrive: Check zero/reference and the physical setup; prepare one model record, keep the answer key teacher-only, and test the intended class access. Use classroom models or supplied data unless an actual fieldhouse survey has been verified.

Language and access: Keep the diagram visible. Offer 60 seconds of partner rehearsal, the lesson frame and these words: highest, lowest, spread, endpoint, zero, evidence. Accept the supported response modes with unchanged criteria.

Recording in the application: Collect responses in the existing lesson, then use teacher review and the existing 1–2–3 target ratings. Observe actual tool handling separately. Preserve the earlier version when a student revises.

Next teaching decision: Ask students to compare a repeated reading against a separate checked reference. Keep the spread and the reference offset as different quantities. Recheck the same idea with a different example before treating it as independently secure.

DAY 2 · SESSION 1.2 · CYCLE 1

Reading the divisions

55-minute short session · one block

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

tr.u1.read-rule. I can read a rule to its marked division and write a whole number, fraction and unit.

Success today: Checkpoint 2 5/8 in. Exit start 1 in, end 4 7/16 in, length 3 7/16 in; second reading 2 19/32 in. Prepared calls (whole inch plus tick/denominator): 0+3/16, 1+8/16, 2+12/16, 3+5/16, 0+14/16, 4+1/16, 1+10/16, 2+7/16, 5+15/16, 0+6/16, 1+9/32, 2+16/32, 0+24/32, 3+19/32, 4+31/32. Answers: 3/16, 1 1/2, 2 3/4, 3 5/16, 7/8, 4 1/16, 1 5/8, 2 7/16, 5 15/16, 3/8, 1 9/32, 2 1/2, 3/4, 3 19/32, 4 31/32 inches.

TimeWhat happens

Diagnostic opening

Students produce: A saved opening response; then 60 seconds of partner explanation using the diagram.

Look/listen for: Counting tick marks instead of intervals, or dropping the whole inch. Have the student point to zero, count the spaces in one inch, name the denominator and then add the whole-inch part.

7–17 min

Explain and model

Teacher: Model aloud: Start 1 in; end 4 3/8 in Length = end reading − start reading 3 3/8 in. The end reading alone is not the length. Ask a student to identify the reference, the unit and the evidence supporting the conclusion.

Students produce: An annotated calculation or reference sketch with quantities and units; a prediction before the investigation.

Look/listen for: A reason for each operation. If students repeat the answer without a method, cover the result and have them point to the given quantities.

17–30 min

Investigation and individual record

Do six readings each; include fractions that simplify. 4. If a rule has thirty-seconds, repeat with it. If not, use the enlarged reference for a separate thirty-seconds check. Rotate measurement/checking roles; observe each student rather than inferring skill from a group result.

Students produce: An individual table with quantities, values, units and evidence source. Label supplied data as supplied; keep unexpected results.

Look/listen for: Have the student point to zero, count the spaces in one inch, name the denominator and then add the whole-inch part.

30–40 min

Drawing and handoff

Look/listen for: The representation agrees with the measurements and can be interpreted without the author supplying missing information.

Individual exit and evidence
